papers.partial_detail: Summary, Introduction (start), Section 4 Large-scale Photonic Quantum Computing, Section 5 Conclusion and Outlook. Sections 2 and 3 (photonic quantum information, photonic quantum computing) skimmed by headings only.
papers.what_it_is: A review chapter on photonic quantum computing, covering discrete-variable and continuous-variable approaches, scaling and error correction.

assertions.value: The review states that photonic quantum computation is largely divided between discrete-variable and continuous-variable approaches, and that the two can be combined in a hybrid CV-DV fashion to overcome the limitations of either approach.
quotes: The field is largely divided between discrete-variable (DV) and continuous-variable (CV) photonic quantum computation.
It is possible to combine both DV and CV in a hybrid CV-DV fashion to overcome the limitations of either approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: The review's own statement of its subject and scope, Summary p.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that photon loss is the largest technological challenge for optical quantum computing schemes, and that the proposed solution is to treat photon loss as a qubit error and use error correction codes.
quotes: The largest technological challenge for optical QC schemes is photon loss.
The solution is to understand photon loss as a qubit error and find error correction codes to reduce the probability for that error
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's assessment in a review, with no single study behind it.

assertions.value: The review states that the error-correction methods developed by PsiQuantum can tolerate a 2.7% probability of suffering a single-photon loss.
quotes: The error-correction methods developed by PsiQuantum can tolerate a 2.7% probability of suffering a single-photon loss(Bartolucci et al. [2023]).
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to a vendor's own published work (Bartolucci et al. 2023), not checked here.
assertions.reader_inference: The 2.7% figure is attributed to the vendor's own error-correction scheme; the review does not restate the conditions under which it holds.

papers.title_in_file: Supervised Similarity for High-Yield Corporate Bonds with Quantum Cognition Machine Learning
papers.what_it_is: A BlackRock and Qognitive study that uses quantum cognition machine learning (QCML) to learn a supervised distance metric between corporate bonds, compared with random forest proximities and Euclidean distance.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the HYG high-yield bond data the QCML metric outperforms the other metrics in k-nearest-neighbors regression, unweighted and proximity-weighted. On the IGSB investment-grade data it outperforms unweighted and performs comparably, if slightly worse, proximity-weighted.
quotes: For the corporate bonds dataset we see in Figure 4 that for HYG, the QCML metric outperforms other metrics for both the unweighted and proximity-weighted methods of KNN regression.
For IGSB, we see that the QCML metric outperforms again for the unweighted KNN regression, and performs comparably, if slightly worse, for the proximity-weighted KNN regression.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on two ETF data sets; the comparison is read from Figure 4, not from tabulated numbers.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's QCML models are trained as classical numerical models of Hermitian operators; no quantum hardware run is reported. The finance application is the identification of tradable alternatives to illiquid bonds.

assertions.value: The authors state that the data are the publicly available holdings of two ETFs, HYG and IGSB, cross-sectional and downloaded at the end of day on 09/18/2024, with a random 80-20 train-test split, and test results repeated over 10 different 80/20 splits.
assertions.anchor: Section 4 Data Description, p.5; Section 5.1, p.6; Section 6.1, p.8
quotes: The holdings data of both ETFs are publicly available. The data features selected are cross-sectional, and they were downloaded at the end of day on 09/18/2024.
We first performed a random 80-20 train-test split of the data, and used the train data for hyperparameter optimization.
We repeated the test over 10 different 80/20 train-test splits of the data
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own data and split, Sections 4, 5.1 and 6.1.
assertions.reader_inference: All results rest on one snapshot date for each of two ETFs.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not claim QCML is uniformly superior to traditional machine learning methods. They also state that the choice of neighbor weighting is largely subjective, and that proximity-weighting inherently favors the random-forest-based proximities.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2, p.7; Section 6.2, p.10; Section 8 Conclusion, p.14
quotes: Although we do not make any claim that QCML is uniformly superior to traditional ML methods, our analysis has shown that there exist multiple contexts in which it can generate superior performance.
the question of which weights one should use is largely subjective and ill-defined
In this respect, proximity-weighting inherently favors the RF-based proximities
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limits, Sections 5.2, 6.2 and 8.

papers.title_in_file: How to find expressible and trainable parameterized quantum circuits?
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section II (metrics, expressibility and start of trainability), Section III experiments (single-objective, hardware search, QNN and VQE case studies), Section IV summary, Appendix A to C. The trainability derivation and later appendices were not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A metric-guided ansatz-search framework for parameterized quantum circuits, with a finite-sample trainability criterion, simulations, a 5-qubit hardware run, and QNN and VQE case studies.

assertions.value: The authors report that in multi-objective searches they reproduce the expected anticorrelation between expressibility and trainability, with highly expressive circuits tending to be poorly trainable, and that the framework can still identify feasible circuits in the joint regime.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Summary and Outlook, p.11
quotes: In multi-objective searches, we reproduce the expected anticorrelation between expressibility and trainability. Highly expressive circuits tend to be poorly trainable
our results show that the framework can navigate this trade-off in a controlled way and identify feasible circuits in the joint expressibility
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from simulated searches in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report an expressibility search on the 5-qubit IQM Spark processor with 50 optimizer iterations on hardware, and state that the discovered ansatz improves over all benchmark circuits within the considered hardware-constrained search space.
assertions.anchor: Section III A Single-objective optimization, p.6; Section IV, p.11
quotes: In addition to simulations, we performed an expressibility search on the 5-qubit IQM Spark
We executed 50 optimizer iterations on hardware.
the discovered ansatz improves over all benchmark circuits within the considered hardware-constrained search space
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one 5-qubit device run in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The search space was restricted to the device's native gates and star topology, so the comparison is within that restricted space, not against unrestricted circuits.

assertions.value: The authors report that the ansatz found by search had favorable metric values but failed to reliably converge to the ground-state energy when deployed in VQE for H2. They state that higher metric scores do not automatically imply improved downstream performance.
assertions.anchor: Section III VQE case study, p.10; QNN case study, p.9
quotes: The ansatz search circuit achieves favorable metric values (Figure 4a). However, when deployed in VQE for H2 it fails to reliably converge to the ground-state energy (Figure 4b).
higher metric scores (or proxies such as effective dimension) do not automatically imply improved downstream performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical negative result from one molecule in one study, stated as a limitation by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's UCCSD-like accuracy claim for H2 depends on switching the gate pool to symmetry-preserving excitation operators, per the summary; the metric-only search did not suffice.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 2 framework, parts of Sections 3 and 4 (ansatz tables and parameter counts), Section 5 comparison with LCU, Section 6 Conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of compiling block-encoding unitaries with variational circuits, with parameter-count scaling, symmetry-restricted ansatze and a gate-count comparison with linear combination of unitaries.

assertions.value: The authors report that the number of variational parameters in the parameterized circuit approaches the number of free parameters in the input matrices, and that variational compilation can achieve an exact encoding using only a single ancilla qubit.
quotes: We find that the number of variational parameters in the parameterized quantum circuit approaches the number of free parameters in the input matrices
We demonstrate that VCBE ansatze can achieve an exact encoding using only a single ancilla qubit.
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical optimization result from one study, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that for Heisenberg Hamiltonians of up to 5 sites VCBE decreases 2 qubit gate counts by more than an order of magnitude compared to LCU, and that for larger systems the 2 qubit counts for LCU seem to be smaller than for VCBE.
quotes: VCBE decreases the 2 qubit gate counts, one of the most important quantum resource metrics, by more than an order of magnitude compared to LCU for this specific case of Heisenberg Hamiltonians of up to 5 sites
For larger systems, the 2 qubit counts for LCU seem to be smaller than for VCBE
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical comparison on one Hamiltonian family; the paper itself says LCU wins at larger sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational compilation of block-encodings ceases to be computationally feasible for large system sizes, and that the heavy classical pre-processing for optimizing the variational parameters remains the key limitation.
quotes: While performing a variational compilation of blockencodings ceases to be computationally feasible for large system sizes
the heavy classical pre-processing associated with optimizing the variational parameters remains the key limitation
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Abstract and Section 6.

papers.title_in_file: Explainable Quantum Machine Learning for Multispectral Images Segmentation: Case Study
papers.version_note: The file name carries the arXiv 2503.08962 listing title (On the status of current quantum machine learning software). The text inside is v3 of that arXiv id, titled Explainable Quantum Machine Learning for Multispectral Images Segmentation: Case Study, which matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A case study of running a hybrid quantum-classical change-detection model on an IBM quantum device, with proposed explainability metrics, software issues and cost estimates.

assertions.value: The authors report a binary classification accuracy of 67.44% on the simulator and 56.70% on the real device, after relabeling. They state the model run on the real device had an untrained quantum layer because the weights were not applied during the forward pass.
quotes: The binary classification accuracy we obtained was 67.44% and 56.70% for the model ran on the simulator and the real device respectively.
Ultimately, the model we ran on the real device, was the one with untrained quantum layer.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one run on one device with an untrained model.
assertions.reader_inference: Because the model was untrained and the labels were flipped after the fact, the numbers say little about trained QML performance on hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that incompatibility with PennyLane prevented use of IQM devices, so they used ibm_brisbane, and that in the time available they classified only 1815 samples using 1024 real device shots for each sample.
quotes: With only IBM devices to select from, we decided to use (ibm_brisbane) for our experiments.
During that time we managed to classify only 1815 samples (918 and 897 of class 0 and 1 respectively) using 1024 real device shots for each sample.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental scope, Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that PennyLane and Qiskit do not fully support noisy simulation of quantum machine learning models, and that for their model and libraries standard gradient-based device-oriented training seemed impossible.
quotes: do not fully support noisy simulation of quantum machine learning models.
the implementation of standard (gradient-based) deviceoriented training seemed impossible.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion from one case study and one software stack.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results suggest QML models run on real devices are highly unreliable, inaccurate and costly, and that they believe current quantum devices of similar class are not ready for running complex ML models.
quotes: Our results also suggest that the QML models ran on real devices are highly unreliable, inaccurate and costly.
We believe that current quantum devices (at least the ones of similar class to the one we tested) are not ready for running complex ML models.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's belief drawn from one untrained-model run.
assertions.reader_inference: The supporting run used an untrained quantum layer, so the claim reaches further than the evidence.

papers.title_in_file: Auto Quantum Machine Learning for Multisource Classification
papers.what_it_is: An automated quantum machine learning (AQML) approach to multisource data fusion, tested on a synthetic MNIST fusion task and on ONERA change detection against classical MLPs and manual quantum models.

assertions.value: The authors report that on ONERA change detection the best classical model reached accuracy 0.752 against 0.743 for the best PQC model, and that the average accuracy of one PQC variant was 0.730 against 0.728 for the MLP.
quotes: While the accuracy of the best classical model outperformed the best PQC model
outperformed MLP, although only slightly
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one data set and a few dozen runs.
assertions.reader_inference: The same section later reports 0.752 as the AQML result against 0.720 originally reported, so the 0.752 figure is attributed differently in two places; the labeling should be checked against the paper before use.

assertions.value: The authors report that the best PQC model found had only 8 trainable parameters, while the MLP they used had 384 trainable parameters.
quotes: This model had only 8 trainable parameters! For the comparison, the MLP we used had 384 trainable parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that none of the models is close to the reported state-of-the-art, and conclude that under similar restrictions AQML-found PQCs give results comparable with classical models.
quotes: While none of the models is close to the reported state-of-the-art, we conclude that given similar restrictions, AQML-found PQCs lead to results comparable with classical models.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit on their results, Section 4.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a synthetic MNIST fusion task manually selected QML models were worse than those found by AQML, and that the AQML models were never as good as the best classical models but needed far fewer trainable parameters.
quotes: Using specially prepared MNIST as an synthetic example, we report that manually selected QML models were worse than that found by AQML.
Although the models were never as good as the best classical models, they were comparable, and they needed far less trainable parameters to achieve their accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result on a three-class synthetic task in one study; per-fold numbers are in Table 3.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Random Features: A Spectral Framework for Quantum Machine Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections II to V (models, numerical simulations, finite-sampling robustness, connections, conclusion). Appendices (RFF background and spectral derivations) skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A proposal of Quantum Random Features and Quantum Dynamical Random Features, fixed-circuit models that mimic random Fourier features, tested in noiseless simulation on image classification.

assertions.value: The authors report that simulations on Fashion-MNIST reach up to 89.3% accuracy. They attribute the 89.3% figure to the RFF-like variant, and state that the computational advantage does not yet manifest in that variant because the exponential cost of constructing W_RFF remains.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section III Numerical Simulations, p.4
quotes: simulations on Fashion-MNIST reach up to 89.3% accuracy
it attains a test accuracy of 89.3%,
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The headline accuracy comes from the QRF-Rff variant, not from the scalable QRF circuit, and the runs are noiseless simulations.

assertions.value: The authors report that as the number of layers increases the test accuracy of QRF gradually converges toward that of the RFF-like variant, and that the required number of layers remains nearly constant as the number of qubits increases.
quotes: As the number of layers L increases, the test accuracy of QRF gradually converges toward that of QRFRff.
Importantly, the required number of layers remains nearly constant as the number of qubits increases.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result across qubit counts in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report from numerical simulation that the deviation between theoretical and empirical accuracy does not scale exponentially in qubit number, and state that in their model the required number of shots does not grow exponentially with the number of qubits.
assertions.anchor: Section III A Robustness Under Finite Sampling, p.5 (Figure 3)
quotes: These findings indicate that in our model, the required number of shots does not grow exponentially with the number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical scaling observation over a limited range of qubit counts, not a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The shot-count scaling is inferred from a trend over roughly 7 to 15 qubits in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that QRF reaches about 53% testing accuracy on CIFAR-10, and that QRF alone does not reach the performance of QERC.
assertions.anchor: Section III, p.4; Section IV, p.6
quotes: The QRF reaches about 53% testing accuracy
However, QRF alone does not reach the performance of QERC.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; QERC is a different published model.

papers.title_in_file: Scalable quantum circuits for exponential of Pauli strings and Hamiltonian simulations
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section IV Conclusion, and the noise-simulation discussion before it. Section II circuit constructions and Section III simulation setups read at the summary level only; proofs not checked.
papers.what_it_is: A circuit design for the exponential of Pauli strings from one-qubit gates and CNOTs, used for Suzuki-Trotter Hamiltonian simulation, with noiseless and noisy simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state as a key derived result that any two Pauli-string operators composed of identity and X gates are permutation similar, with the permutation matrices being products of CNOT gates with the n-th qubit as control, so the circuits are implementable on low-connected hardware.
quotes: A key result we derive is that any two Pauli-string operators composed of identity and X gates are permutation similar, and the corresponding permutation matrices are product of CNOT gates, with the n-th qubit serving as the control qubit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a derived result in the Abstract and developed in Section II; the reader did not check the proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that simulations for systems of up to 18 qubits show the circuit approximation closely matches the exact evolution, with errors comparable to the numerical Trotterization error.
quotes: Simulations for systems of up to 18 qubits show that the circuit approximation closely matches the exact evolution, with errors comparable to the numerical Trotterization error.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one study, for specific Hamiltonian classes.

assertions.value: The authors report, for noisy simulations of systems of up to 8 qubits, that the fidelity between noisy and noiseless outputs drops down to the 0.8 mark at the end of the time evolution for certain states, and that the choice of input state matters significantly.
quotes: assess the efficiency of the circuit models in NISQ computers for systems of up to 8 qubits governed by time-independent
drops down to the 0.8 mark during the end of the time evolution for certain states
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result under an assumed noise model, from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the circuits were used to simulate time-independent and time-dependent 1D Hamiltonian operators, and that reducing gate counts by clustering commuting Pauli strings is left to future work.
quotes: several time-independent and time-dependent 1D Hamiltonian operators
The number of quantum gates for Hamiltonian simulation can be reduced by clubbing the commuting Pauli-strings into clusters before applying the Suzuki-Trotter formula.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of the tested scope and of what remains undone, Section IV.
